activities.caption: find the faulty line in this tillage ledger
activities.name: agTillageSpot

config.prompt: A student weighs land preparation methods. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Conventional tillage clears weeds, incorporates residues and creates a fine seedbed.
Its cost is exposing organic matter to oxidation and leaving bare ground to rain — erosion's opening bid.
Erosion rates under conventional practice typically run BELOW soil formation rates, so topsoil slowly deepens.
No-till saves passes in fuel, labour and hours, which is decisive at scale.
Land clearing is the other side of the ledger: land-use change is a major emissions source.
config.correction: Erosion under conventional practice typically EXCEEDS soil formation rates by factors of ten to a hundred — topsoil that takes centuries to form can wash away in a decade.
config.why: That gap is what makes preparation method a genuine intergenerational decision rather than a stylistic one.

activities.caption: bet on the hazard of uniformity
activities.name: agBlightPredict

config.q: In 1970, US Southern corn leaf blight exploited a single shared cytoplasm across most hybrid maize. What was the cost?
choices: Under 1% of the crop, absorbed by insurance
About 15% of the crop — genetic uniformity turning one pathogen into a systemic event
Nothing, because hybrids are individually resistant
It only affected subsistence varieties, not commercial hybrids
config.why: About 15% of the crop. Pests and pathogens thrive in genetic uniformity — the structural hazard behind every monoculture risk.

activities.caption: true or false — the access economy
activities.name: agSenJudge

statements.s: Famines occur only when regional food production falls short.
statements.why: Sen showed, case by case (including the Bengal famine of 1943), that famines occur with food PRESENT — people starve for lack of access.

statements.s: Entitlement analysis asks who can buy, at what price, through what shock.
statements.why: Wages, prices, distribution and politics — not regional production totals.

statements.s: Cash crops always undermine food security.
statements.why: The evidence is mixed and case-specific: cotton revenues can buy staples, or extraction can undermine them.

statements.s: Food security and nutrition security are distinct design targets.
statements.why: Micronutrient deficiency coexists with calorie sufficiency, and obesity now coexists with underweight in the same countries.

activities.anchor: a hermetic (airtight) bag or metal silo
activities.caption: guess what a few dollars of container saves
activities.name: agStorageEstimate

config.prompt: A smallholder stores a tonne of grain in a traditional woven store and loses roughly a quarter to insects, rodents and moisture. Roughly what percentage loss does a hermetic bag or metal silo cut that to?
config.why: Down to a few percent. At household scale that is the difference between selling a surplus and buying food back at post-harvest prices — the classic poverty trap, closed by a container costing a few dollars.
config.context: Roughly a quarter lost against a few percent — the cheapest calories are the ones already grown.

activities.anchor: cash crops are the cause of hunger
activities.caption: work the security triad
activities.name: agSecurityBranch

config.root: A drought hits, and the exporting countries respond by restricting wheat and rice exports. World prices spike. Which leg of the food-security triad does this test, and who bears it?

start.text: Availability, access, stability — the price crises of 2007–08 and 2021–22 broke one leg hardest. Which one, and for whom?

choices.label: Availability — there was not enough grain grown
choices.feedback: Production was not the binding constraint; the supply existed and moved.

choices.label: Stability — the shocks, plus access for import-dependent countries
choices.feedback: The import-dependent countries, not the food exporters, bore the hunger.

availability.text: The grain existed. Export bans and disrupted shipping rearranged who could reach it — which is an access and stability story wearing an availability mask.

stability.text: Drought plus export bans plus the Black Sea disruption sent prices sharply up, and the import-dependent countries bore it. Dashboards now track stocks, import dependence, dietary diversity and real food prices the way finance tracks risk.

config.why: Security has three legs: availability, access and stability. The design question is never just how much is grown — it is who can buy, at what price, through what shock.

activities.anchor: roughly a third of food produced is never eaten
activities.caption: pair each region's waste with its remedy
activities.name: agWasteMatch

config.prompt: Where the loss happens determines what fixes it. Match each to its lever:

pairs.right: hermetic storage bags, rural roads, solar cold rooms

pairs.left: richer countries — consumer and retail waste
pairs.right: labelling reform, dynamic pricing, redistribution, norms
retail standards and confusion around best-before dates

pairs.left: livestock products' land and water per calorie
pairs.right: diet composition — the EAT-Lancet shift toward plants

config.why: In poorer regions the highest-return investments are unglamorous infrastructure; in richer ones they are labels, pricing and norms. The demand side holds the single biggest lever.

activities.anchor: well under a tenth of the total
activities.caption: which curve shows what actually dominates a meal?
activities.name: agFootprintTrace

config.prompt: Relative greenhouse-gas footprint per kilogram of food. Which curve shows the shape the lesson describes — where what you eat dwarfs where it came from?

curves.label: a gentle rise — transport and distance dominate
steep exponential — a few foods an order of magnitude above the rest

config.xlabel: food type (low → high impact per kg)
config.why: Beef's footprint per kilogram is many times that of beans regardless of where either was grown, and season can beat distance — tomatoes grown locally in heated greenhouses can out-emit shipped field tomatoes. Transport is typically a tie-breaker, not the driver.

config.text: The FAO projection underlying the 2050 debate is demand growth of roughly half — about %%0%%–60% over 2005/07 levels — not a doubling. Roughly %%1%% billion people are expected on a warming plateau, and yield gaps (smallholders often harvesting half or less of attainable yields) are the supply-side opportunity.
config.hint: The lower bound of the 50–60% range; and the population figure the lesson names for 2050.

activities.anchor: up to a thousand years for a few centimetres
activities.caption: guess the soil clock before the reveal
activities.name: agSoilClockEstimate

config.prompt: At best, how many years does it take to form a few centimetres of topsoil?
config.why: Up to a thousand years for a few centimetres — centimetres per century at best. That makes soil the least renewable resource agriculture uses: losses are measured in decades, gains in generations.
config.context: A thousand years for a hand's depth — the climate clock and the soil clock run at the same speed.

activities.anchor: the top metres hold more carbon than the atmosphere
activities.caption: true or false — soil as a climate pool
activities.name: agSoilCarbonJudge

statements.s: Soil is a carbon pool of the same order as the atmosphere and vegetation combined.
statements.why: The top metres hold more carbon than the atmosphere, so soil management is climate management.

statements.s: The agronomy of building soil and the climate practice of sequestering carbon are the same operations.
statements.why: Cover crops, residue return, manure and compost, reduced tillage, diverse rotations — one toolkit, two framings.

statements.s: Soil organic matter is only a carbon account, with no bearing on fertility.
statements.why: It is simultaneously the fertility asset — water-holding, nutrient exchange, structure — and the carbon account.

statements.s: Moving soil organic carbon by one percentage point can be done within a season.
statements.why: It takes years of inputs, which is the honest caveat on every organic-matter rule of thumb.

activities.caption: file each nitrogen outcome by its ledger
activities.name: agNitrogenLedgerBuckets

config.prompt: The fertiliser economy has a climate double edge. File each item:

items.label: nitrous oxide at about 273× CO₂'s warming per kilogram
right rate, time, place and form
legumes fixing atmospheric nitrogen in a rotation

config.why: If only a third of applied nitrogen is harvested, two-thirds is the emission-and-pollution budget — every percentage point of efficiency gained is a proportional saving.

activities.anchor: a warmer atmosphere holds about 7% more water
activities.caption: fill the physical constant behind heavier storms
activities.name: agErosionCloze

config.text: Rainfall intensity is rising with warming: a warmer atmosphere holds about %%0%%% more water per degree, so the same slope loses more soil per storm. No-till with residue cover commonly cuts soil loss by an %%1%% of magnitude versus bare conventional ground.
config.hint: A single digit from the Clausius–Clapeyron relation; and the phrase that means 'ten times'.

activities.caption: put the methane saving on the scale
activities.name: agRicePlace

config.prompt: Alternate wetting and drying lets rice paddies drain mid-season. Place the typical methane reduction reported in field trials.
config.why: Field trials commonly land in the 30–50% range, sometimes more, while saving water and largely holding yield — one of the few practices that scores on all three climate-smart objectives at once.

config.q: A region converts all its irrigation to drip, which is 90%+ efficient. What did the water saving do to aquifer depletion?
choices: It reversed the decline, since less water was withdrawn per hectare
It often accelerated depletion, because the saving funded more irrigated land and thirstier crops
It had no measurable effect either way
It eliminated the need for allocation rules entirely
config.why: Efficiency gains often increase consumption — the rebound effect, measured repeatedly in efficient-irrigation programmes that accelerated depletion. Water saved per hectare is real; water saved by the basin depends on what the saving funds.

activities.caption: find the faulty line in this organic-vs-conventional ledger
activities.name: agClimateOrganicSpot

config.prompt: A student weighs organic farming's climate case. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: The accounting is genuinely two-sided, so the label alone settles nothing.
Organic fields cut on-farm emissions — no synthetic nitrogen, whose manufacture is energy-intensive — and build soil carbon.
Typical organic yields run a fifth HIGHER, so feeding the same population needs less land.
Land-use change (forests converted) emits far more than the fertiliser saved.
Per unit of product some organic crops come out ahead and some behind.
config.correction: Typical organic yields run roughly a fifth LOWER, so feeding the same population needs MORE land — which is where the land-use change emissions come from.
config.why: The climate-smart synthesis borrows from both toolkits — legumes, rotations, organic inputs where they work — without treating the label as the objective.

activities.caption: scale the unit of management up to the watershed
activities.name: agWatershedBranch

config.root: Each farm in a watershed irrigates efficiently. The aquifer is still falling under a pump-race — the Ogallala, the North China Plain, northwestern India.

start.text: Every individual decision looks rational. Where does the fix have to sit?

choices.label: At the farm — keep pushing per-hectare efficiency
choices.feedback: That is what every farm is already doing, and the aquifer is still falling.

choices.label: At the watershed — allocation limits plus collective management
choices.feedback: Groundwater user associations and shared irrigation schedules are the governance analogue of the agronomy.

farm.text: Efficiency improves again, the pump-race continues, and the rebound effect converts the saving into more irrigated land.

watershed.text: Efficiency and a cap together: water saved per hectare is real, and water saved by the basin depends on what the saving is allowed to fund.

config.why: Upstream extraction empties downstream deltas, so the climate-smart unit is the watershed. Pair efficiency with allocation limits — technology plus a cap, not technology alone.
